[[File:VogtsTheorem-OrigMod.png | thumb|right | WIki, Illustration to Vogt's theorem.]]'''Vogt–Russell theorem''' is a hypothesis in [[Stellar astrophysics]] stating that the structure of a star in hydrostatic and thermal equilibrium is determined solely by its '''total mass''' and '''chemical composition'''.<ref name="CarrollOstlie">Carroll, B. W.; Ostlie, D. A. (2017). ''An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics'', 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|978-1-108-42216-1}}.</ref> The idea dates back to 1926 when [[Heinrich Vogt (astronomer)]] formulated the theorem with internal communications and seminars. Its first publication only appeared in 1931.<ref name="Vogt1931">Vogt, H. (1931). "Zur Theorie des Sternaufbaues". ''Astronomische Nachrichten''. 244: 49–56. [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1931AN....244...49V ADS].</ref> Independently, [[Henry Norris Russell]] developed the same theorem in the early 1930s.<ref name="Russell1931a" />

As numerical modelling techniques improved, researchers discovered that the relationship is not universal and that the equations of stellar structure can yield multiple solutions for the same set of global parameters.<ref name="KWW2012" /> Thus, the “theorem” is treated today as a local approximation, valid mainly for main-sequence stars and under physical conditions without extreme effects.<ref name=":0">{{Cite arXiv |last=Gautschy |first=Alfred |date=2018 |title=The theorem that was none - II. The profound 70s |class=astro-ph.SR |eprint=1812.11864}}</ref>

== History ==
The original formulation of the principle attributed to [[Heinrich Vogt (astronomer)]] dates from 1926, but there is no publication from that year. The first formal exposition appears in his 1931 article in [[Astronomische Nachrichten]], in which he discusses how the constitution of a star in hydrostatic and thermal equilibrium depends essentially on total mass and chemical composition.<ref name="Vogt1931"/>

Independently, [[Henry Norris Russell]] published in 1931 two technical articles in the [[Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society]], analyzing how the internal [[Stellar structure]] and global parameters such as radius and luminosity are determined by these same two fundamental parameters, total mass and chemical composition.<ref name="Russell1931a">Russell, H. N. (1931). "Notes on the Constitution of the Stars". ''Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society''. 91: 951–958. [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1931MNRAS..91..951R ADS].</ref><ref name="Russell1931b">Russell, H. N. (1931). "Notes on the Constitution of the Stars: Addendum". ''Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society''. 92: 147–150. [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1931MNRAS..92..147R ADS].</ref>

Russell presented more detailed versions of these ideas in review articles on the [[Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada]] in 1933.<ref name="Russell1933">Russell, H. N. (1933). "The Constitution of the Stars". ''Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada''. 27: 375–394. [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1933JRASC..27..375R ADS].</ref> These works consolidated the notion later called the “Vogt-Russell theorem,” despite not providing a mathematical proof of uniqueness.

== Formulation ==
The theorem states:

''The internal structure of a star in hydrostatic and thermal equilibrium, including profiles of pressure, temperature, density, and luminosity, as well as its observable global parameters, radius and luminosity, would be uniquely determined by the total mass'' <math>M</math> ''and the initial chemical composition'' <math>X_i</math>.

This formulation use the four fundamental equations of [[Stellar structure]]: [[hydrostatic equilibrium]], mass conservation, energy transport, and energy conservation to construct the main proposition.<ref name="CarrollOstlie" /> If one assumes, sphericity, absence of significant rotation, absence of strong magnetic fields, and thermal equilibrium, the system is mathematically well-conditioned and, in principle, admits a single continuous solution that satisfies the boundary conditions at the center and at the surface.<ref name="KWW2012" />

== Modern interpretation ==
Numerical studies developed from the second half of the twentieth century onward showed that, under some conditions like near structural limits such as the [[Schönberg–Chandrasekhar limit|Schönberg-Chandrasekhar limit]], or in cases involving instabilities, multiple mathematical solutions may exist for the same values of <math>M</math> and <math>X_i</math>.<ref name="KWW2012">Kippenhahn, R.; Weigert, A.; Weiss, A. (2012). ''Stellar Structure and Evolution'', 2nd ed. Springer. {{ISBN|978-3642303040}}.</ref> These solutions may include stable and unstable states, indicating that the originally postulated uniqueness is not universal.<ref name="KWW2012" /><ref name=":1">{{Citation |last=Kähler |first=Helmuth |chapter=The Vogt-Russell Theorem, and New Results on an Old Problem |date=1978 |title=The HR Diagram |pages=303–311 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-009-9851-3_56 |access-date=2025-11-17 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-9851-3_56 |doi-broken-date=22 December 2025 |isbn=978-90-277-0906-6|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref>

For most stars under normal conditions like nondegenerate main-sequence stars, numerical solutions do indeed converge to a single stable solution. This explains:

* the narrow band occupied by stars with the same mass and composition in the [[Hertzsprung–Russell diagram]];<ref name="CarrollOstlie" /> 
* the good agreement with the [[Mass–luminosity relation]];<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fernandes |first1=João |last2=Gafeira |first2=Ricardo |last3=Andersen |first3=Johannes |date=2021 |title=Revisiting the mass- and radius–luminosity relations for FGK main-sequence stars |url=https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202040035 |journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics |volume=647 |pages=A90 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361/202040035 |arxiv=2103.11044 |bibcode=2021A&A...647A..90F |issn=0004-6361}}</ref>
* the good agreement of [[Stellar evolution]] models that use only <math>M</math> and <math>X_i</math> as initial parameters.<ref name="CarrollOstlie" />

Thus, although the theorem is not strictly valid as a general law, it remains fundamental as a practical first approximation in stellar astrophysics.<ref name="KWW2012" /><ref name=":1" />

== Limitations ==
The theorem fails when:<ref name="KWW2012" />
* the star is near structural limits (e.g., the [[Schönberg–Chandrasekhar limit|Schönberg-Chandrasekhar limit]]);
* there is significant rapid rotation;
* strong magnetic fields influence energy transport;
* strong electron degeneracy is present;
* the star is not in thermal equilibrium.

In these regimes, multiple solutions arise, invalidating uniqueness.<ref name=":0" />
